title: Cities and Islands Where Cats Belong
seoTitle: Cat Cities and Islands: History & Care | BHOC Veterinary
description: From the Hermitage to Tashirojima: ten stories of cats, local history and animal welfare, with photographs, dated figures and sources.
deck: Ten stories about animals that became part of a place, and the people who care for them.

paragraphs: At the Hermitage gates, on the stone steps of Syros and among Rome's ancient ruins, cats live alongside human history. Sometimes they become part of it. People know their names, put them on postcards and dedicate museums and celebrations to them. Behind that affection are people who fill bowls, notice illness and help an animal find a home. Their daily care gives these places their meaning.

places.name: The Hermitage, Saint Petersburg
places.heading: Hermitage Cats: Saint Petersburg
places.subtitle: A Tradition Older Than the Museum

image.alt: A tabby-and-white Hermitage cat sits on a stone ledge beside the museum's iron gate in Saint Petersburg.
image.caption: A Hermitage cat beside the museum gate. Saint Petersburg, 2010.

places.countScope: Museum cats. A figure in 2023 exhibition materials; no verified 2026 census was located.
paragraphs: In 1745, Empress Elizabeth ordered cats to be brought from Kazan to protect palace rooms from rodents. The tradition continued into the life of the Hermitage Museum.

The cats became a museum symbol, with people responsible for their care, veterinary support and their own celebration, the Day of the Hermitage Cat. Alongside great works of art, there is an enduring place for living animals and their needs.
places.care: Museum staff and volunteers supporting the Hermitage cats.

places.name: Istanbul
places.heading: Istanbul Cats
places.subtitle: Neighbours Known Around the World

image.alt: Cats rest around a painted green shelter beside a stone wall on a street in Istanbul.
image.caption: Street cats and their shelter in Istanbul, 2011.

places.countScope: Street cats across the city. An undated GoTürkiye estimate, checked 24 October 2026; not a census.
paragraphs: In Istanbul, cats are part of everyday neighbourhood life. There is a tangible record of this care: a 1714 engraving depicts a man taking food for cats to the city's market.

Today, residents leave water and food and provide shelters. A cat can have a place in the life of an entire courtyard through the attention of people who see it at their door every day. That relationship has become one of Istanbul's most recognisable images.
places.care: Neighbourhood residents, local volunteers and municipal veterinary services.

places.name: Torre Argentina, Rome
places.heading: Torre Argentina Cats in Rome
places.subtitle: A Home Among Ancient Temples

image.alt: A cat walks between ancient brick and stone ruins at Largo di Torre Argentina in Rome.
image.caption: A cat among the ruins of Largo di Torre Argentina, Rome.

places.countScope: Sanctuary cats described in a published visitor account. A secondary-source indication, not a verified 2026 total.
paragraphs: After excavations in 1929, stray cats found shelter among the ruins of Largo di Torre Argentina. Local women, known in Italy as gattare, brought them food. In 1993, Lia Dequel and Silvia Viviani began the work that grew into the well-known sanctuary.
Its story now includes care for sick and older cats, sterilisation and adoption. Among stones that preserve ancient Rome, an everyday story of human commitment continues.
places.care: Torre Argentina Cat Sanctuary and its volunteers.

sources.label: Torre Argentina Cat Sanctuary: Who We Are

places.name: Kotor
places.heading: Kotor: The City of Cats
places.subtitle: A Feline Presence in an Old Port

image.alt: A tabby-and-white cat sits against a stone wall beside a paved lane in Kotor's Old Town.
image.caption: A cat in the Old Town of Kotor, 2018.

places.countScope: Old Town cats in a travel feature. No reliable current census was located; Kotor Kitties' sterilisation totals are not a city population count.
paragraphs: Cats on its stone lanes have become an unofficial symbol of Kotor. Local tradition connects their arrival with visiting ships; this is a story passed down, rather than a documented origin. The Cats Museum opened in the Old Town in 2013.
Kotor Kitties began in 2018 as a small effort to sterilise cats. Behind the familiar feline shapes beside the city walls is the shared work of residents, volunteers and veterinarians.
places.care: Residents, Kotor Kitties / Kotorske Mačke and local veterinarians.

places.name: Iraklia
places.heading: Cats of Iraklia
places.subtitle: Care After the Summer Ends

image.alt: Fishing boats lie beside the waterfront path at Agios Georgios harbour on Iraklia, Greece; no cats are visible.
image.caption: Agios Georgios harbour, Iraklia, 2019. A photograph of the setting; no cats are visible.

places.countScope: Sterilised cats supported by Cats of Iraklia, as reported by partner GCWS; checked 24 October 2026. A project figure, not an island census.
paragraphs: On this small Cycladic island, cats live around the port, villages and beaches. For Cats of Iraklia, the defining question was who would feed and treat them after the visitors left. Local nurse Kyriaki-Kia founded the project in 2017.

Behind the beautiful island setting is year-round work: winter feeding, sterilisation and journeys to a veterinarian on neighbouring Naxos. A few committed people can make a lasting difference to animals' lives.
places.care: Cats of Iraklia, island volunteers and the Greek Cat Welfare Society.

sources.label: Greek Cat Welfare Society: Cats of Iraklia

places.name: Syros
places.heading: The Cats of Syros
places.subtitle: One Kitten Changes a Home

image.alt: A black-and-white cat and a ginger cat walk over shallow stone steps in an alley on Syros.
image.caption: Cats on the stone steps of Syros, 2021.

places.countScope: The site's population in its 2024 year-end review. The project separately fed 70 street cats in Kini, rising to 100 in winter. No island-wide total is established.
paragraphs: In 2010, Joan Bowell and her husband Richard had just settled into their home on Syros when a sick kitten appeared in the garden. Helping that kitten became the beginning of God's Little People Cat Rescue. Joan rescued 30 cats in the first year.

Syros Cats also works on the island, caring for resident animals, feeding street cats and arranging sterilisation. Behind the familiar pictures of cats on island steps are people who have made care part of their daily lives.
places.care: Syros Cats, God's Little People Cat Rescue and local caretakers.

places.name: Su Pallosu, Sardinia
places.heading: Su Pallosu Cats: Sardinia
places.subtitle: A Shoreline Story That Continues Through Care

image.alt: Sandy shoreline at Putzu Idu on Sardinia's San Vero Milis coast, with shallow waves, small yellow boats, coastal houses and distant cliffs.
image.caption: Nearby Putzu Idu on the wider San Vero Milis coast, Sardinia, 2012. Coastal setting; the Su Pallosu cat colony is not shown.

places.countScope: Caretaker's statement of 5 February 2026. All had been abandoned here; this is not the former native colony's population.
paragraphs: Su Pallosu became known through photographs of cats beside the sea. Behind those images are the Atzori family's home and years of care. In early 2026, the caretaker reported that the original locally born colony had come to an end after its last native cat died.
Rescued cats, abandoned here in earlier years, remain in daily care with Andrea Atzori. That care continues for the cats living here today.
places.care: Andrea Atzori; the I Gatti di Su Pallosu project history.

places.name: Tala, Paphos District
places.heading: Tala Cats: Paphos, Cyprus
places.subtitle: From Feeding Near a Monastery to a Sanctuary

image.alt: A garden courtyard with stone paths, architectural fragments and an arcaded building at Agios Neophytos Monastery in Tala, Cyprus; no cats are visible.
image.caption: Agios Neophytos Monastery courtyard in Tala, 2023. The neighbouring monastery, rather than the cat sanctuary itself.

places.countScope: According to the Tala Cats website, checked 24 October 2026. It uses both 'approximately 500' and '500+'; no census date is given.
paragraphs: Stray cats had long lived near Agios Neophytos Monastery. In 2011, Dawn and Mark Foote began visiting once a week to feed them. Care soon became a daily commitment, and dozens of cats needing treatment were staying in their home.

Donations made fencing possible in 2013. Tala Cats gradually developed into a sanctuary with shelters and separate spaces for vulnerable animals. A large care project grew from a simple commitment to return and help again.
places.care: Tala Cats, Dawn and Mark Foote, staff and volunteers.

places.name: Tashirojima
places.heading: Tashirojima Cat Island
places.subtitle: An Island with a Cat Shrine

image.alt: Nekotarou, a tabby-and-white cat on Tashirojima, rests with its paws tucked under its body on an outdoor paved surface.
image.caption: Nekotarou, a cat on Tashirojima, 2014.

places.countScope: Island-wide figure in a Japanese transport bureau report dated 17 March 2026. A rounded description, not a published individual register.
paragraphs: Neko Jinja, a cat shrine, stands near the centre of Tashirojima. Local tradition describes cats as guardians of a good catch, a story preserved by Ishinomaki City as part of island culture.

Island residents feed and look after the cats. A 2026 government visitor project explains that tourists must not add their own feeding, so the residents can maintain managed care. Respect for this place includes listening to the people who live with its animals throughout the year.
places.care: Island residents and local partners in care and visitor education.

places.name: Houtong, New Taipei
places.heading: Houtong Cat Village
places.subtitle: A New Chapter for a Mining Village

image.alt: Three cats rest on a lane beside potted plants at Houtong Cat Village in Taiwan.
image.caption: Three cats at Houtong Cat Village, Taiwan, February 2026.

places.countScope: Official statement of 8 April 2024. A new count was announced in February 2026; no verified replacement total was located.
paragraphs: As the coal industry declined, Houtong lost residents. Its cats, photographs shared by enthusiasts and the work of volunteers helped the village gain a new identity. The district's account links the cat village's emergence with improvements to the surroundings and care for the animals.

Houtong now has a Cat Office. In February 2026, Taiwan SPCA resumed operating it with local volunteers and the city's animal protection service. Each day begins with feeding and a roll-call of cats known by name.
places.care: Houtong Cat Lovers' Society, Taiwan SPCA and New Taipei's animal protection office.

countNote: Every figure has a date and a defined scope. City estimates, sanctuary residents and cats supported by a project are different populations. Where no recent census was found, this is stated explicitly.
closingHeading: The Care That Continues After the Photograph
closing: Each story continues through ordinary acts: clean water, a safe place to sleep, sterilisation, vaccination, relief from pain and the search for a home. Respect for animals becomes real through these decisions. For BHOC Veterinary, this is where a story that matters begins: with attention to an individual life and responsibility for its welfare.
principle: Respect for animals becomes real through daily care.

supportAdvice: Read local visiting and feeding guidance. On Tashirojima, residents provide managed feeding and visitors are asked not to add food.
Support recognised local groups through their official channels, including sterilisation, vaccination and veterinary-care programmes.
Give cats space to rest and move away, and follow each site’s rules for photography and interaction.
Contact the local rescue organisation about adoption or volunteering, so help matches the animals’ needs.
